title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
claim: Compatibility of a model pair can be predicted before training by combining two cheap scores derived from local neighborhood overlap.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; numbered headers; formula box and ranked table at end
description: Three numbered panels read left to right. Panel 1, "Which pairs are the most compatible?", lists five vision encoders (INet-21K, DINOv2, MAE, CLIP, CLIP) as colored boxes. Each is paired with a language model (LLaMA, BLOOM, OLMo, RoBERTa) through a double arrow with a question mark. The colors show the training paradigm, explained in a legend. Panel 2 shows two scatter plots of representation spaces X (vision) and Y (language). Each has a query point i inside a dashed circle of colored shapes that are its nearest neighbors. Below the plots is the k-NN overlap formula o_i^(k). Panel 3 starts with a green box, "Compatibility ≈ Ease × Ceiling". Arrows lead to two boxes, Ease (pair-specific) and Ceiling (paradigm-level), then to a red-outlined table. The table ranks the pairs with green and red ease and ceiling values and regime labels (act now, budget-limited, ceiling-limited, incompatible).
caption: Given a library of candidate encoders, the compatibility of a model pair is typically unknown before running the downstream transfer. Using COMPASS, we estimate the compatibility based on local neighborhood agreement: for each probe sample, we compare its local k-NN overlap across the two representation spaces. Aggregating this local overlap across different axes gives two scores computed before alignment or merging. Ease is a pair-specific score that measures how close the selected pair is at the start of the relevant dynamics: before encoder training in cross-modal alignment, and before weight merging in task arithmetic. Ceiling is a paradigm-level score that estimates how much agreement the corresponding training paradigms can support on average. Candidate pairs are ranked by combining ease and ceiling. Each axis is thresholded at its median value: green compatibility scores are above the corresponding median while the red ones are below it. The resulting high/low pattern assigns each pair to one of four regimes: act now (high ease, high ceiling), budget-limited (low ease, high ceiling), ceiling-limited (high ease, low ceiling), or incompatible (low ease, low ceiling).
abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
